findings.title: getBaseConditions returns an unparenthesized OR fragment, so appended predicates change meaning
findings.body:
When there are no filters, `getBaseConditions()` returns the authorization fragment as-is. For org and team scopes that fragment is `(A) OR (B)` (built by the reduce at lines 171-174 and 204-207) with no outer parentheses.

The natural way to use it is `WHERE ${base} AND "createdAt" >= ${start}`. That renders as `(A) OR (B) AND createdAt...`, which Postgres parses as `A OR (B AND createdAt...)`. Every extra predicate (date range, status, etc.) then silently skips the team-booking branch, so insights counts come out wrong.

The old Prisma object API could not have this problem. The service should wrap every fragment it returns, e.g. `Prisma.sql\`(${authConditions})\``, so callers can compose it safely.

findings.title: Public filter fragment `(eventTypeId = X) OR (eventParentId = X)` has no outer parentheses; naive AND-combination bypasses authorization
findings.body:
With a single eventTypeId filter, `getFilterConditions()` (a public method) returns `("eventTypeId" = X) OR ("eventParentId" = X)` with no outer parentheses.

`getBaseConditions` wraps it correctly. But any caller that combines the public fragments itself, e.g. `WHERE ${auth} AND ${filter}`, gets `auth AND (eventTypeId = X) OR (eventParentId = X)`. Postgres evaluates that as `(auth AND eventTypeId = X) OR eventParentId = X`. Every booking whose eventParentId matches is then returned regardless of the authorization condition, leaking other users' and teams' bookings.

The service should return self-contained, parenthesized fragments. The new tests lock in the unwrapped form.

findings.title: Public `findMany` removed without a replacement query method
findings.body:
The public `findMany(findManyArgs)` method is deleted and replaced with `getBaseConditions()`, which only returns a SQL fragment.

Any existing consumer of `InsightsBookingService.findMany` will stop compiling. Each caller now has to hand-write raw SQL against `"BookingTimeStatusDenormalized"`, which multiplies the composition and precedence risks above.

The PR does not update any callers and does not say whether any exist. Either keep a query method that applies the conditions internally, or confirm and update all call sites.

findings.title: Unreachable fail-open fallback returns filter conditions without authorization
findings.body:
`getAuthorizationConditions()` always returns a `Prisma.Sql` object, which is always truthy. So the `else if (filterConditions) return filterConditions;` and `else return NOTHING_CONDITION` branches can never run.

The structure is also dangerous: if the auth builder is ever changed to return null or undefined, this code fails open and returns filter-only conditions with no authorization restriction. Remove the dead branches, or make the missing-auth case return NOTHING_CONDITION.

findings.title: Caching tests deleted although caching logic is unchanged
findings.body:
The whole "Caching" describe block was removed. `getAuthorizationConditions` and `getFilterConditions` still memoize via `cachedAuthConditions` and `cachedFilterConditions`, but nothing tests that behavior any more.

The tests could have been converted to the Prisma.sql format like the others. The single DB-backed test only covers user scope; org and team scope SQL is never executed against the database. Malformed SQL in those branches, such as the `= ANY(...)` array binding or the `isTeamBooking` column, would go undetected. The author also notes the tests were not run.
